title: Less is More: Simplicity in Teamwork
author: Heather McGonigal
summary: Coach Heather McGonigal argues that one of a leader's main responsibilities is to make it easier for people to do great work. She observes that the systems built to help teams succeed, such as extra meetings, approval steps, and tracking tools, often end up getting in the way, because each addition makes a new demand on people's time and attention. She frames simplification as removing obstacles and adding clarity, not as lowering accountability or expectations. She also reminds leaders that they do not have to have all the answers, since the people doing the work know where things get stuck, provided the environment is psychologically safe enough for them to say so. Her concrete invitation is to ask the team, at the next meeting, what one thing could be simplified, changed, or stopped, then choose one idea to try and follow through. This is the fourth video in her Coach Heather Fundamentals series on simplification.
points: Complexity has a cost: every added meeting, process, or reporting requirement draws on finite human energy, so leaders should ask what to subtract before adding more.
Simplifying is framed as clarity and removing obstacles, explicitly not as squeezing more work out of people or relaxing accountability.
Teams hold the best information about what slows them down, which makes the team a think tank for simplification.
Psychological safety is the condition that lets people question an existing process and suggest a different one.
The practical move is a single question at the next team meeting, followed by one small experiment that the leader actually follows through on.
quotes: Here’s something I’ve seen time and again in my work coaching leaders and teams: Sometimes the very systems we’ve created to help people succeed end up getting in their way.
But every additional meeting, process, or reporting requirement makes another demand on someone’s time and attention. Our people are our most valuable resource, and their energy is not unlimited.
Some of the best insights about what’s slowing a team down come from the people doing the work every day. They know where things get stuck.
When people feel comfortable questioning an existing process or suggesting a different approach, we gain access to the collective intelligence of the team.
What’s one thing we could simplify, change, or stop doing that would make it easier for all of us to do our best work?
Remember, simplification isn’t about squeezing more work out of people. It’s about removing what gets in the way of people doing their best work.
